title: Taking the Long View of the M Coupe’s Departure

body_markdown:
I am going to beg forgiveness for writing yet a third piece about the sale of my 1999 BMW M Coupe (the “clown shoe”). No, I’m not phoning it in. No, the well of Hack inspiration hasn’t run dry. I owned the car for 20 years. There were thoughts to be thunk, and things to be said. Cut me some slack, eh?


As I shared in the piece I wrote a few weeks ago, my son Ethan asked if he could take the car for a final drive before the new owner picked it up. Ethan had only driven it once—at least, that I was supposed to know about—in 2012, and I thought about the two of us recreating the mad dash into Boston we took in the car in 2010 to get his short film submitted to a contest before the deadline. We didn’t do that, but I did hand him the keys on a clear Saturday morning and request that he be hyper-careful and stay on lightly trafficked roads, as it would really suck if the car were damaged after I’d accepted a deposit and the check for the balance was on the way. Nothing happened; Ethan was grateful, all good.


The next question was whether *I* was going to take the M Coupe on a farewell drive. I expected that I would, as I have a line in a song of mine about how last-time-you-do-something endings should be memorable, sharp, and clear. But I didn’t. I’d barely driven the car the past five years, so I didn’t feel like I needed to manufacture an artificial ending. I was content to let it sit in the garage until the buyer came. And that’s what I did.


The next day, the new owner and his wife drove out from Albany, New York, to pick up the car. He and I passed papers, I loaded a few spare parts into the back, and we each took photos of the other one behind the car’s beautiful planted rear end before he hit the road.


This will have to qualify as an ending for my time with the M Coupe.


Rob Siegel


But at some point during the pleasantries, the buyer said, “I’m surprised your son didn’t want it.” (He had met Ethan while he was in the house.) I laughed at the prospect, but I didn’t really think anything of the comment at the time. Not until the buyer was gone did I begin mulling over what had just happened and wondering why selling a cool car I’d owned for nearly 20 years was such a nothing-burger to me.


Let’s start with why I didn’t keep the car for my kids. My daughter, Eryn, 32, lives in Somerville, Massachusetts, with her fiancé, is studying to become a radiological technician, and is the one of my three kids who never learned to drive a stick (a near-miss with a parked car and oncoming traffic while she was learning spooked her). She’s happy driving what was my mother’s 2013 Corolla, which is the perfect car to leave parked on Somerville streets and may outlast the cockroaches. She fixes certain things when they break (she replaced the climate-control panel when it futzed out), but isn’t a “car person.” Plus, *all* the cars except the Armada are sticks, and she’s never mentioned lusting after any of them.


My middle son, Kyle, 36, is an artisanal metalworker living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. His lone intersection with the M Coupe was the night of his high school prom, when he asked if I could photograph him and his prom date next to it. He’s still driving the 1990 Toyota Tacoma my mother and Maire Anne and I bought him when he graduated college. The past five years, he’s gotten heavily into vintage mopeds (yes, that’s totally a thing). He’s a very cool guy, and I have no doubt that he’d look dope AF cruising Santa Fe in the M Coupe and carving canyons out in the boonies. But he’s never asked about winding up with any of my cars. And from a practical standpoint, he has no garage, which isn’t ideal if you own a car like this.


Ah, youth.


Rob Siegel


Cars haven’t really risen to the top of Ethan’s (38) list of interests, though he uses my 2003 E39 530i a *lot* (he lives with us) *,* and he appreciates how nice it is. He intersected twice with the M Coupe, first when he asked if he could borrow it for his prom—and was miffed at me when I told him no, for risk and insurance reasons—and again when it was used in the short film he made in 2010. Since the car has been in storage most of the last five years, it’s not like it’s been a constant presence in the driveway calling to him like a siren that escaped from *The Odyssey* . But he certainly knew I still had it, and was aware that I was selling it. He’s a very direct person, and if he wanted to talk to me about buying it, or ask the blunt question—“Dad, can you keep the clown shoe so that when you die I can inherit it?”—he would’ve done so. Curiously, like his brother, Ethan has recently gotten into both vintage mopeds (he bought a 1979 PA50 Honda Hobbit) and e-bikes.


I didn’t think Ethan still had the short film in which the M Coupe was used, but he did. As I referred to two weeks ago, this is the actor seconds before he nearly pulled out into an oncoming car.


Ethan Siegel


Still, once the subject of the car not going to one of my kids came up via the innocent question from the buyer, I was surprised that I hadn’t even considered that outcome as a possibility. I guess the reason is that, other than the 40-year-owned BMW 3.0CSi, I don’t regard the cars as assets. They’re just my cars. They come and go. I don’t need to ask anyone’s permission or to solicit anyone’s thoughts before selling them. Maybe with the M Coupe, I should have.


Now, the other issue: Why wasn’t selling a cool car I’d owned for 20 years more traumatic? The answer is more nuanced than, “Well, I hadn’t been driving it anyway.”


It was nearly 35 years ago that I first wrote the following in a BMW CCA *Roundel* magazine column: “It is my professional opinion that a car nut with a family needs at least three cars: A van/minivan/wagon in which to haul the stuff of life; a satisfying road sedan; a pampered classic; a roadster; a driver’s school go-cart; a four-wheeler, and a project car. Like I said, seven cars. All you wackos out there can tell your spouses I said it was all right.” This came to be known as “Siegel’s Seven-Car Rule” (SSCR). I returned to it over and over. And as my car count crept up to 14, I adroitly stuffed eight cars into the slot innocently labeled “project car.”


[In this Hagerty piece](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-perspective-of-the-not-a-collector/) a few years ago, I noted a failure of SSCR—namely, that not all of the so-called slots represent actual activities. I, who have waxed a car maybe four times in my life, laugh out loud at the idea of “pampering.” Most notably, there aren’t slots for “car to road-trip to vintage car events” and “satisfying car to pleasure-drive.” Some combination of the pampered classic, the driver’s school car, and the project car fits these bills, but the issue is more complicated than that. Cars are best when they’re actually *for* something. If they’re not, then you’re collecting, whether you admit it or not. Since I stubbornly and honestly insist that I’m *not* a collector, this created a collision between my self-image and reality.


As I thought about it, this was the root of the issue with the M Coupe. Its unforgivingly stiff, back-pain-producing seats had long ago ruled it out for road trips; I never even considered driving to the annual[Schuh Syndikat](https://schuhsyndikat.org/) clown shoe events. Although I quit doing high-performance driving events decades ago, I still used to enjoy taking out the M Coupe and hitting the nearby cloverleaf ramps on I-95, but in 2013 I had an inner-ear event that made the lateral and vertical *g* -forces of aggressive driving unpleasant, so that was out of the picture as well. The occasional runs out to the Fitchburg and then Monson storage spaces, and exercising the car a few times a year around the edge of the Berkshires, seemed to be all that the M Coupe was “for.”


But what about just taking pleasure drives in it? A pleasure-driver may not be one of my seven slots, but it’s definitely a thing. That role got usurped by the two vintage Lotuses—first the 1974 Europa Twin Cam Special, then the ’69 Elan +2. As I’ve said repeatedly, these cars are fabulous for tooling through the leafy twisty roads just west of here, doing 42 mph in a 35 zone, and feeling like you should be arrested for the amount of fun you’re having. The M Coupe was the opposite. Exceed a local speed limit by 20 mph, and it says, “Geez, get *on* me, grandpa!”


So, yeah—the quickest, best-handling, and sexiest car I own, the one whose rear-quarter view connotes forward motion better than any other car BMW has ever built, lost its passion-spot in the stable to two buzzy, British, Lots-Of-Trouble-Usually-Serious bolt buckets. Passion is a fickle mistress.


Did I *really* supplant the M Coupe with the Europa and then the Elan +2? Sort of.


Rob Siegel


When I had this epiphany after the M Coupe departed the premises, I pulled the Elan +2 out of the garage and took it for a pleasure drive. Rattles? Check. Thunks and clunks? Check. A punch list as long as my arm? Check. Cheshire Cat grin on my face? Oh, that’s a big check. Those moments when you look at and drive a car and think, “I still can’t believe that I own this thing” usually tail off with time, but after two years of owning the +2, that sentiment is still shiny and new. The Europa is in storage, but I have no doubt that I’ll still hear the siren’s song when I drive it on a twisty road through dappled autumn sunshine.


When I got back home, I texted the buyer to ask if he and the M Coupe had gotten home safely. He sent me two pics of the car next to his 2002 on his bucolic-looking property outside Albany, and wrote: “They look so good together. Such a contrast, but also meant to be friends and share a garage.” I immediately thought about last year’s sale of my 1973 Bavaria and my 1979 Euro 635CSi, and this spring’s sale of my hot-rod 2002 Bertha, all of which are now out in the world being enjoyed by their owners. How can this not be a better situation for the M Coupe than sitting unused in storage?


It’s like it’s in the Elysian Fields.


Travis K.


So it all makes sense. At least to me. Of course, my kids might be carrying on a group text where the other two of them are ragging on Ethan: “You’re the one living at home! I can’t *BELIEVE* you let Dad sell the M Coupe!”


***
